The standard reduction potentials for the two half-cells are given below.\\
$\mathrm{O_2(g)}+4\mathrm{H^+(aq.)}+4e^-\to2\mathrm{H_2O}(\ell)$, $E^\circ=1.23$ V,\\

\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SA13-P2-CHEM-S1-G1-2, source={Score Advanced - Test 13 (13 May 2023)}, questions={1-2}]
A secondary cell after use can be recharged by passing current through it in the opposite direction so that it can be used again. A good secondary cell can undergo a large number of discharging and charging cycles. The most important secondary cell is the lead storage battery commonly used in automobiles and invertors. It consists of a lead anode (negative terminal) and a grid of lead packed with lead dioxide (PbO$_2$) as cathode (positive terminal). A 38\% solution of sulphuric acid is used as an electrolyte.\par
The cell reactions when the battery is in use are given below :\par
\textbf{Anode :} Pb(s) + SO$_4^{2-}$(aq) $\rightarrow$ PbSO$_4$(s) + 2e$^-$\par
\textbf{Cathode :} PbO$_2$(s) + SO$_4^{2-}$(aq) + 4H$^+$(aq) + 2e$^-$ $\rightarrow$ PbSO$_4$(s) + 2H$_2$O($\ell$)\par
i.e., overall cell reaction consisting of cathode and anode reactions is :\par
Pb(s) + PbO$_2$(s) + 2H$_2$SO$_4$(aq) $\rightarrow$ 2PbSO$_4$(s) + 2H$_2$O($\ell$)\par
On charging the battery the reaction is reversed and PbSO$_4$(s) on anode and cathode is converted into Pb and PbO$_2$, respectively.\par
\end{bankpassage}
